scores.fix: Hardly anyone plays AI songs, yet fake plays can still get paid. Frame 0: FEW REAL LISTENERS. FAKE PLAYS CAN STILL GET PAID.
scores.note: Two sentences, 14 words and a Never-say: most AI songs earn nothing and caught fakes are stripped out, so 'they still take money from your favourite artist' and ARTISTS PAY leave a false belief.

scores.fix: Some days, over half the new songs on one app are AI. Frame 0: ONE APP, SOME DAYS: HALF THE NEW SONGS ARE AI.
scores.note: 'Half' holds only on peak days (39-44% on average), 'aren't human' edges toward 'songs nobody wrote', frame 0 drops 'one app' into half of all new music, and uploads don't move the money anyway.

scores.fix: Keep the line; frame 0: 18 MONTHS FOR HAVING BOTS PLAY HIS AI SONGS.
scores.note: The fact file's own safe wording about one real person; frame 0 should keep 'AI' and '18 months', and the payoff has to air that his harm is contested.

scores.fix: An AI song can get paid without a single real listener.
scores.note: True with 'can' and a straight road to the pot, but it leaves the AI-song fuss off frame 0.

scores.fix: Bots playing AI songs can shrink your favorite artist's paycheck.
scores.note: Plain, true with 'can', payoff on frame 0; the video must size 'shrink' as a little, by an amount nobody has measured.

scores.fix: Your monthly fee also pays songs you've never heard.
scores.note: A true pro-rata reveal, but the honest answer to 'which songs?' is mostly other people's real favorites, so the stakes only arrive with the bot turn.

scores.fix: Keep; make frame 0 match the voice: WHO PAYS WHEN A BOT PLAYS AN AI SONG?
scores.note: A safe question whose honest two-part answer is the payoff; it is L35 with a singular voice that doesn't match its plural frame 0.

scores.fix: Why would anyone upload AI songs just for bots to play?
scores.note: Fair (one app says fake plays are the main reason AI songs get uploaded), but 'make' should be 'upload' and AI is missing from the hook.

scores.fix: On one app, most plays on AI songs were fake. Frame 0: ONE APP, 2025: MOST AI SONG PLAYS WERE FAKE.
scores.note: Scoped and past tense, fair per FL 2.4, but a plural stat headline with a slow start.

scores.fix: Bots want a slice of the billions streaming pays artists.
scores.note: 'Spotify's $11 billion payout' paints one giant pot (it is per country, per month), puts Spotify in a bot frame, and frame 0 never says whose billions.

scores.fix: On one app, AI songs' biggest fans were bots. Frame 0: ONE APP: AI SONGS' BIGGEST FANS WERE BOTS.
scores.note: The voice is scoped, but 'are' rests on 2025 data and frame 0 drops 'one app', so the take-away is that AI songs' audiences are fake everywhere.

scores.fix: Your favorite artist can end up sharing the pot with bots.
scores.note: 'Splitting the pot' suggests an even or big share and 'is' asserts it now, with no 'slip through' and no size.

scores.fix: One app says its ~90,000 daily AI songs are mostly for bots.
scores.note: 'Mostly for bots' is one app's assessment stated as fact, and frame 0 drops 'one app' and 'nearly'.

scores.fix: Keep the voice; frame 0: BOTS FAKE THE PLAYS. THE MONEY'S REAL.
scores.note: The voice is honest ('skim' sizes it right), but AI SONGS. FAKE PLAYS. REAL MONEY. equates AI songs with fraud.

scores.fix: You can't always spot AI songs, and apps can't always spot bots.
scores.note: Two sentences that blur AI detection into bot detection, and APPS MISS BOTS TOO implies apps miss as often as listeners do.

scores.fix: Some of your streaming fee can end up with bots (same words on frame 0).
scores.note: True with 'some' and 'can', but frame 0 drops 'some', so the whole fee looks at risk.

scores.fix: When bots play AI songs on repeat, who pays?
scores.note: A good question, but stated as a general habit it leans toward 'bot fraud is an AI problem' (most fraud one app caught wasn't on AI songs).

scores.fix: Keep; credit 'Deezer/Ipsos, 2025' small on frame 0 and turn to fake plays by line 2.
scores.note: Frame 0 is the fact file's scoped blind-test wording and the question is the fuss itself, but the mechanism isn't in it, so the payoff needs a hard turn.

scores.fix: Some of your subscription can end up paying a bot farm.
scores.note: True on both surfaces ('part of', 'can') and personal without making the viewer the loser; at 12 words it is at the limit.
True (FL 4.16, 3.11), but frame 0 carries no stakes, and why a paying bot hurts anyone takes longer than 3 s to explain.

scores.fix: One app says most AI uploads are for bots, not you.
scores.note: Attributed only in the voice; frame 0 states one app's view as a universal fact, and 'made' should be 'uploaded'.

scores.fix: Keep; frame 0: BOTS THAT SLIP THROUGH SHRINK YOUR ARTIST'S SLICE.
scores.note: The truest statement of the mechanism, but the qualifier and 'slice' cost punch, and the pot has to be on frame 0.
The fact file's safe wording almost word for word and beyond attack, but mild, and the bots only arrive in line 2.

scores.fix: You might already like an AI song, and that's not the problem.
scores.note: True and the fairest to AI-using artists, but the video can't answer 'which one?' and the hook points away from the mechanism.
True (2017-2024, four services) and close to home; the video must not let 'for years' read as the apps waving it through.

scores.fix: On one app, AI songs' biggest fans were bots.
scores.note: Universal and present tense on one app's 2025 data, and unfair to AI acts with real fans.

scores.fix: Bots played his AI songs billions of times; he got 18 months. Frame 0 credit: prosecutors say.
scores.note: Until the bots appear it reads as prison for a popular AI musician, and 'billions' is the prosecutors' figure stated as fact.

scores.fix: An AI song no real person hears can still get paid.
scores.note: True with 'can', but the hear/play hinge needs 'fake plays' in line 2, or leavers think unheard songs earn just by existing.

scores.fix: If real people barely play AI songs, who does?
scores.note: 'Somebody's playing all these AI songs' is false for most of them (they get almost no plays), and frame 0 overgeneralizes.

scores.fix: Real people barely play AI songs, so why upload so many?
scores.note: A fair question on the fact file's safe wording, but frame 0's LOTS OF BOTS is a different, unattributed claim, and it reads slowly.

scores.fix: Nearly half of one app's new songs are AI, and barely played.
scores.note: Scoped and about right (44% on average), but two numbers, and frame 0 has neither 'AI' nor 'one app'.

scores.fix: Keep the voice; frame 0: ONE APP: MOST AI UPLOADS ARE FOR BOTS.
scores.note: Attributed in the voice, but frame 0 states one app's assessment as a universal fact.

scores.fix: Keep the voice; frame 0: ONE APP, 2025: UP TO 85% OF AI SONG PLAYS FAKE.
scores.note: Scoped in the voice; frame 0 drops 'one app' and '2025', and 'up to' will be heard as a flat 85%.

scores.fix: Bots can skim your favorite artist's pay.
scores.note: Punchy, and 'skim' is honest about size, but 'are skimming' asserts uncaught fraud nobody has measured, exactly where a fact-checker attacks.
The safest strong line: no claim to attack, it rides the AI fuss, and the honest answer (nobody if caught, every real artist a sliver if not) is the payoff.

scores.fix: Keep the voice; frame 0: SOME OF YOUR SUBSCRIPTION CAN END UP WITH BOTS.
scores.note: True in the voice, but frame 0 drops 'some', so the whole subscription seems to go to bots.

scores.fix: What fake plays earn comes out of real artists' pay.
scores.note: The zero-sum payoff in seven words, but the comma can be misread as 'real artists don't earn', and bots' own fees make it gross, not net.

scores.fix: Keep; frame 0: HIS BOTS PLAYED HIS AI SONGS. WHO LOST OUT?
scores.note: The fairest way to use Smith (the contested harm asked, not asserted), but clunky and slow on frame 0.

scores.fix: You'll never hear the fake plays that thin artists' pay.
scores.note: True and eerie, but 'the plays that cost artists money' is vague without 'fake' and asserts a loss nobody has measured.

scores.fix: Keep; frame 0 credits him: FAKE PLAYS? 'A ZERO-SUM GAME' (APPLE MUSIC'S BOSS).
scores.note: Verbatim, in context and one real person, but 'zero-sum' is jargon, an executive isn't relatable, and frame 0 credits the brand, not him.

scores.fix: One man's own math: 1,000 bots, $1.2 million a year. Frame 0: HIS MATH: 1,000 BOTS, $1.2M A YEAR. THEN 18 MONTHS.
scores.note: Accurate as his own projection, but the frame 0 equation reads as a current going rate and glamorizes a crime before the 18 months arrive.

scores.fix: He had bots play his AI songs instead of fans: 18 months.
scores.note: True and plain (the prosecutor's own 'bots in the place of consumers'), but it drops AI, the fuss the topic was picked for.

scores.fix: Prosecutor says he 'robbed' artists; his lawyers say no artist lost out.
scores.note: Attribution covers it legally, but leading with one side of a contested harm leaves 'artists were robbed' as the take-away, and HIS BOTS 'ROBBED' changes the quote's subject.
True (AFP) and a strong human chill, but it is impersonation, which the pot can't pay off (FL 5.14), so as the core it is a bait-and-switch; use it as the fuss beat.

scores.fix: Keep; frame 0: HIS TRICK: TONS OF AI SONGS, A FEW BOT PLAYS EACH.
scores.note: His own plan, fairly paraphrased, but frame 0 loses 'his' and 'bots', and the video must say Spotify's 1,000-play rule now blunts it.
Single-source (TIME) impersonation the pot can't pay off, and 'her' is unexplained on frame 0.

scores.fix: Every fake play that slips through shrinks your favorite artist's share.
scores.note: Hayduk's logic, but blaming 'AI slop' makes AI the thief (the problem is fraud, not AI), 'slop' and 'pads' are jargon, and frame 0 is definite.
